# Migrating and Troubleshooting Documents {#sec-rmd-workflow} The converted paper rendered without an error, and the PDF went to the co-authors. In the methods section, 'as Figure 2 shows' had become `?@fig-flow shows`, and three other references pointed at nothing, because the chunk labels had kept their old R Markdown names. Nobody noticed for a week, because a clean render looks exactly like a correct one. This chapter is about the work around a literate document rather than inside it: converting between formats, migrating a project, placing floats in a PDF, and diagnosing a render, both the failure that stops it and the one that does not. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *Programs must be written for people to read, and only incidentally for machines to execute.* [Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman]{.smallcaps}, *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* (1985) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: converting, migrating, and debugging documents is work on the Report stage, where code and derived data become the document a reader sees.](12-rmd-workflow_files/figure-html/fig-rmd-workflow-pipeline-1.png){#fig-rmd-workflow-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Report.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 20 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-quarto for documents, chunk options, cross-references, and `freeze`. The code uses `knitr`, which Quarto installs with R support, and calls each function with its namespace (`knitr::spin()`), so it needs no `library()` call. The debugging example runs the `quarto` command-line tool. **You'll be able to.** - Convert between `.R`, `.Rmd`, and `.qmd` with `knitr::spin()`, `knitr::purl()`, and `knitr::convert_chunk_header()`, and state what each leaves for you to do by hand. - Decide whether an R Markdown project should be migrated, and detect the cross-references a conversion breaks without an error. - Control where LaTeX places figures and tables in PDF output. - Diagnose a failing render from its log, and find the silent failures a successful render can hide. **Outline.** - [Converting between formats](#sec-rmd-workflow-convert) - [Migrating an R Markdown project](#sec-rmd-workflow-migrate) - [Float placement in PDF](#sec-rmd-workflow-floats) - [Engines and other languages](#sec-rmd-workflow-engines) - [Troubleshooting a render](#sec-rmd-workflow-troubleshoot) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-12. 1. What is the quickest way to convert an existing `.R` script into an `.Rmd` or `.qmd`, preserving comments as prose? 2. Why do tables and figures in rendered PDFs often appear in unexpected places, and what do `fig.pos` and `tbl-pos` do? 3. How do you ensure that a figure or table label defined in a document is clickable (hyperlinked) in both the HTML and the PDF outputs? ::: ## Converting between formats {#sec-rmd-workflow-convert} A project that mixes `.R` scripts, `.Rmd` reports, and `.qmd` papers is harder to maintain than any one of them. Pick a primary format (`.qmd` for new work) and convert to it, and convert early: a 100-line document converts in minutes, and a 1,000-line one takes an afternoon of checking. This section uses a short HF-HOME script, written to a temporary directory so that the conversions below run for real. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} work <- file.path(tempdir(), "convert") unlink(work, recursive = TRUE) dir.create(work) writeLines(c( "#' # HF-HOME: primary outcome by arm", "#' Read the randomization list and the outcomes.", "trial <- merge(read.csv('data/randomization.csv'),", " read.csv('data/outcomes.csv'))", "#' Observed risk of the primary outcome in each arm.", "#+ risk-by-arm, echo = FALSE", "tapply(trial$event_30d, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE)" ), file.path(work, "analysis.R")) ``` ::: ### `.R` to `.qmd` with `knitr::spin()` In a script written for `spin()`, a comment that begins `#'` is prose, a comment that begins `#+` holds chunk options for the code that follows, and everything else is code. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} invisible(knitr::spin(file.path(work, "analysis.R"), knit = FALSE, format = "qmd")) cat(readLines(file.path(work, "analysis.qmd")), sep = "\n") ``` ```` #> # HF-HOME: primary outcome by arm #> Read the randomization list and the outcomes. #> #> ```{r} #> trial <- merge(read.csv('data/randomization.csv'), #> read.csv('data/outcomes.csv')) #> ``` #> #> Observed risk of the primary outcome in each arm. #> #> ```{r risk-by-arm, echo = FALSE} #> tapply(trial$event_30d, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE) #> ``` ```` ::: `format = "Rmd"` writes an `.Rmd` instead. Notice that the `#+` line became chunk options in the old in-brace style, not `#|` lines; the next step moves them. ### `.Rmd` to `.R` with `knitr::purl()` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} invisible(knitr::spin(file.path(work, "analysis.R"), knit = FALSE, format = "Rmd")) invisible(knitr::purl(file.path(work, "analysis.Rmd"), output = file.path(work, "extracted.R"), documentation = 0, quiet = TRUE)) cat(readLines(file.path(work, "extracted.R")), sep = "\n") #> trial <- merge(read.csv('data/randomization.csv'), #> read.csv('data/outcomes.csv')) #> #> tapply(trial$event_30d, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE) ``` ::: `documentation = 1` (the default) also writes each chunk header as a comment but drops the prose; `2` keeps the prose as roxygen-style `#'` comments. ### `.Rmd` to `.qmd` by renaming Rename the file, then optionally rewrite the chunk headers with `knitr::convert_chunk_header()`. In a repository, the rename is `git mv paper.Rmd paper.qmd`, so that Git records the history as one file's; here it is a copy. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} invisible(file.copy(file.path(work, "analysis.Rmd"), file.path(work, "paper.qmd"))) knitr::convert_chunk_header(file.path(work, "paper.qmd"), output = file.path(work, "paper.qmd"), type = "yaml") cat(readLines(file.path(work, "paper.qmd")), sep = "\n") ``` ```` #> # HF-HOME: primary outcome by arm #> Read the randomization list and the outcomes. #> #> ```{r} #> trial <- merge(read.csv('data/randomization.csv'), #> read.csv('data/outcomes.csv')) #> ``` #> #> Observed risk of the primary outcome in each arm. #> #> ```{r} #> #| label: risk-by-arm #> #| echo: false #> tapply(trial$event_30d, trial$arm, mean, na.rm = TRUE) #> ``` ```` ::: There is no `quarto convert` step here. That command converts between `.ipynb` and `.qmd`; given an `.Rmd` it writes Jupyter notebook JSON into whatever file you name, `paper.qmd` included. Quarto renders a renamed `.Rmd` with knitr as it stands, so the rename alone produces a working document. The `convert_chunk_header()` call moves options such as `echo = FALSE` and `fig.cap = "..."` out of the braces into `#| echo: false` and `#| fig-cap:` lines. It does not add the `fig-` prefix to labels or touch cross-references. @tbl-rmd-vs-quarto lists what the rename and `convert_chunk_header()` handle, and what is left for you. | Aspect | R Markdown | Quarto | Converted for you? | |---|---|---|---| | Output format | `output: html_document` | `format: html` | No | | Chunk options | In the braces: `{r name, echo = FALSE}` | One option per line at the top of the chunk, as `label: name` and `echo: false` after the comment prefix | Yes, by `convert_chunk_header()` | | Option names | `fig.cap`, `fig.pos` | `fig-cap`, `fig-pos` | Yes, by `convert_chunk_header()` | | Figure and table labels | Any chunk name | Must begin `fig-` or `tbl-` to be referenceable | No | | Cross-references | `\@ref(fig:scatter)` | `@fig-scatter` (syntax in @sec-quarto-chunks) | No | | Book configuration | `_bookdown.yml` and `_output.yml` | One `_quarto.yml` | No | : What changes between R Markdown and Quarto, and what the conversion tools do. {#tbl-rmd-vs-quarto} ### `.ipynb` to and from `.qmd` ```bash quarto convert notebook.ipynb -o notebook.qmd quarto convert notebook.qmd -o notebook.ipynb ``` For collaborators who prefer Jupyter, this conversion is lossless: text becomes Markdown, code becomes cells, and metadata round-trips. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} A model can convert a long document faster than you can, provided you forbid the wrong tool and define 'converted' as a check. > **Context.** Below is an R Markdown file from a `bookdown` > project, with knitr chunk options in braces and > `\@ref(fig:...)` and `\@ref(tab:...)` cross-references. > > **Constraints.** Produce a `.qmd`. Do not use or suggest > `quarto convert`, which is for Jupyter notebooks. Change no > code inside chunks and add no prose. Move chunk options to `#|` > lines, add the `fig-` or `tbl-` prefix to every label that is > cross-referenced, and rewrite every reference to `@fig-...` or > `@tbl-...`. > > **Criteria.** List every label you renamed. The output contains > no `\@ref(`, and every `@fig-` and `@tbl-` reference has a > matching label. *Failure mode.* Models invent connecting prose, tidy the code while they are in it, or rename a label without updating every reference to it. *Check.* Diff the code chunks against the original (`knitr::purl()` both files with `documentation = 0` and compare), then render and run the two counts in the Verification of @sec-rmd-workflow-migrate. The document's text and code are structure; keep the data out of the prompt (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You rename `paper.Rmd` to `paper.qmd`, run `convert_chunk_header()`, and render. The render succeeds. What has not been converted, and how would you find out? **Answer.** The YAML (`output:` still has to become `format:`), every label that lacks a `fig-` or `tbl-` prefix, and every `\@ref()` cross-reference. Neither step touches them, and none of them stops the render. Grep the source for `\@ref(` and the rendered output for `?@`, as @sec-rmd-workflow-migrate shows. ::: ### Exercises 1. Which lines of `analysis.R` does the round trip through `spin()` and `purl(documentation = 0)` fail to reproduce, and why? ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} setdiff(readLines(file.path(work, "analysis.R")), readLines(file.path(work, "extracted.R"))) #> [1] "#' # HF-HOME: primary outcome by arm" #> [2] "#' Read the randomization list and the outcomes." #> [3] "#' Observed risk of the primary outcome in each arm." #> [4] "#+ risk-by-arm, echo = FALSE" ``` ::: Every prose line (`#'`) and the chunk-option line (`#+`). `spin()` turned the prose into Markdown and the `#+` line into chunk options, and `purl()` with `documentation = 0` extracts only code. With `documentation = 2` the prose returns as `#'` comments. ::: ## Migrating an R Markdown project {#sec-rmd-workflow-migrate} The conversion above is a file operation. Migrating a *project* is a different exercise, and the first question is whether to do it at all. ### Whether to convert The reflex is to say yes, on the grounds that Quarto is the successor and current tools are better than superseded ones. That reflex is wrong often enough to be worth resisting, because it mistakes currency for value. A finished analysis that renders correctly under a pinned environment already does everything this book asks of it. Migrating it produces the same output from newer machinery, and in exchange you accept a window in which the document does not render and the numbers have not yet been checked against the old ones. There is no reproducibility argument for the change, and there is a small reproducibility argument against it. @fig-rmd-migrate is the decision. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-rmd-migrate %%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart on whether to migrate an R Markdown %%| project. If the document is finished and published, leave it. %%| Otherwise, if a Quarto-only capability is needed, convert. If %%| not, a third question asks whether the document will grow or %%| change hands: yes leads to convert, no leads back to leaving %%| it alone." %%| fig-cap: "Whether to migrate an R Markdown project. Currency is %%| not a reason on its own. The cases that justify the work are a %%| document that is still growing, a Quarto-only capability you %%| actually need, or a handover to someone who will maintain it %%| after you." flowchart TD A{"Is the document
finished and published?"} A -->|"Yes"| B["Leave it
it renders; migration
buys nothing"] A -->|"No"| C{"Do you need a
Quarto-only capability?"} C -->|"Yes"| D["Convert
multi-language, freeze,
cross-format fidelity"] C -->|"No"| E{"Will it grow, or
change hands?"} E -->|"Yes"| D E -->|"No"| B ``` Anything tagged at submission (@sec-git-solo) belongs in the left branch without further thought. The tagged commit is the record of what was reported, and it should render with the toolchain that produced it. ### What the rename leaves for you Renaming the file and running `knitr::convert_chunk_header()` handles the chunk headers. Neither touches the YAML (`output:` still has to become `format:`), neither touches cross-references, neither knows that a project is a `bookdown` project, and neither audits what your packages assumed about knitr. Budget for those by hand. Quarto is also stricter about labels than `bookdown` was. A figure is only referenceable if its label carries the `fig-` prefix, a table if it carries `tbl-`. A chunk named `scatter` that was addressable as `fig:scatter` under `bookdown` becomes addressable as nothing at all until it is renamed `fig-scatter`. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **Cross-references fail silently.** A `\@ref(fig:scatter)` left unconverted does not stop the render. It emits a broken reference into the output, and a document with thirty figures can acquire a dozen of them without a single error. A reference whose syntax you updated but whose target label you did not (`@fig-scatter` pointing at a chunk still named `scatter`) renders as `?@fig-scatter`, with a warning in a log nobody reads. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} After converting, count the old references left in the source and the unresolved references Quarto wrote into the output. Both counts must be zero. From the project root (display-only): ```r src <- unlist(lapply(list.files(pattern = "[.]qmd$", recursive = TRUE), readLines)) sum(grepl("\\@ref(", src, fixed = TRUE)) out <- unlist(lapply(list.files("_book", pattern = "[.]html$", recursive = TRUE, full.names = TRUE), readLines)) sum(grepl("?@", out, fixed = TRUE)) ``` The second count catches the converse error, a reference whose syntax you updated but whose target label you did not. Change `_book` to your project's output directory. ::: **Package assumptions are the quiet cost.** Code that reached around `knitr` rather than through it does not convert, because there is nothing to convert: it simply behaves differently. The recurring cases are `kableExtra`'s LaTeX-specific options, any output format in the `bookdown::` namespace, and custom `knit_hooks`. Each has to be replaced rather than translated. ### `bookdown` projects A single `.Rmd` is a file. A `bookdown` project is a build system, and it is the case most readers who want to migrate actually have. The mapping is mostly mechanical. `_bookdown.yml` and `_output.yml` collapse into the single `_quarto.yml` of @sec-quarto, chapter files are listed under `chapters:` rather than inferred from filenames, and `index.Rmd` becomes an ordinary `index.qmd` whose YAML carries the book metadata. Part divisions, which `bookdown` expressed as a specially formatted heading, become `part:` entries. What is not mechanical is the numbering. Cross-file references, chapter numbers appearing in prose, and any figure numbered by hand will all move, and they will move silently for the same reason described above. The discipline that makes this tractable is to convert one chapter at a time and keep the `bookdown` build working until the Quarto build matches it. Render both, and compare the outputs rather than trusting that a clean render means a correct one. A clean render means the document compiled. ### The boundary you may not control Migration is rarely unilateral. A co-author may still be editing `.Rmd` in RStudio, a journal template you depend on may exist only as an `rticles` output format, and a continuous-integration workflow (@sec-ci) may invoke `rmarkdown::render` on a path that no longer exists. Each of these is a reason the sensible unit of migration is a project rather than a file: converting half of something leaves two toolchains to maintain, which is worse than either one alone. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A converted chapter renders cleanly, and a grep of the source finds no `\@ref(`. Is it safe to ship? **Answer.** Not yet. The source check finds references in the old syntax; it cannot find a new-syntax reference to a label that was never renamed. Grep the rendered output for `?@` as well, and compare the chapter's figure and table numbers with the `bookdown` build, because numbering moves silently too. ::: ### Exercises 2. The `bookdown` fragment below is to become Quarto. Count the references to convert, and name the labels to rename. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fragment <- c( "As \\@ref(fig:flow) shows, most exclusions were at screening.", "Baseline characteristics are in Table \\@ref(tab:baseline).", "```{r flow, fig.cap = 'CONSORT flow'}", "```{r baseline}", "Outcomes by arm are in \\@ref(fig:outcomes)." ) cat(fragment, sep = "\n") ``` ```` #> As \@ref(fig:flow) shows, most exclusions were at screening. #> Baseline characteristics are in Table \@ref(tab:baseline). #> ```{r flow, fig.cap = 'CONSORT flow'} #> ```{r baseline} #> Outcomes by arm are in \@ref(fig:outcomes). ```` ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} refs <- unlist(regmatches(fragment, gregexpr("\\\\@ref\\([^)]+\\)", fragment))) refs #> [1] "\\@ref(fig:flow)" "\\@ref(tab:baseline)" "\\@ref(fig:outcomes)" ``` ::: Three references, to become `@fig-flow`, `@tbl-baseline`, and `@fig-outcomes`. The chunks `flow` and `baseline` must be renamed `fig-flow` and `tbl-baseline`. There is no chunk for `outcomes` in the fragment: find it before converting, or the converted reference will render as `?@fig-outcomes`. ::: 3. Take a `bookdown` project, your own or any public one, and convert a single chapter of it to Quarto while leaving the `bookdown` build working. Render both and compare the chapter's output. (This changes files in that project; work on a branch.) ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} A complete conversion leaves both counts in the Verification above at zero and the same figure and table numbers in both builds. Expect breaks that produced no message in either render: references to labels in other chapters, which resolve only when the whole Quarto book is built, and numbers typed into the prose. Record each break and whether any message reported it. ::: ## Float placement in PDF {#sec-rmd-workflow-floats} The frustration: you cite a figure in your prose and it appears two pages later. LaTeX treats figures and tables as **floats** and moves them to avoid awkward white space and bad page breaks. For a paper, let it; readers expect floating figures. For a report meant to be read top to bottom, force placement where the figure is declared. The right default depends on the audience. The fix in knitr Rmd: ````Rmd ```{{r demographics, fig.cap = "Demographics", fig.pos = "H"}} plot(...) ``` ```` Or globally: ```r knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.pos = "H") ``` In Quarto, `fig-pos` is a figure option rather than an execution option, so it goes under the PDF format (or in a single chunk as `#| fig-pos: "H"`): ```yaml format: pdf: fig-pos: "H" ``` `H` is from the `float` LaTeX package, meaning 'place exactly here, do not float'. Add to the YAML: ```yaml header-includes: - \usepackage{float} ``` For tables, the equivalent is `tbl-pos: 'H'` in Quarto or `kable_styling(latex_options = "HOLD_position")` in knitr+kableExtra. @tbl-rmd-float-pos lists the placement codes. | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | `h` | Here, if possible | | `t` | Top of a page | | `b` | Bottom of a page | | `p` | On a separate page of floats | | `!` | Prefix: override LaTeX's usual limits on float placement | | `H` | Exactly here, never float (requires the `float` package) | : LaTeX float-placement codes. The default, `htbp`, lets LaTeX choose among the first four in that order. {#tbl-rmd-float-pos} For HTML output, float placement is irrelevant; figures appear in source order. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** You write 'Figure 3 shows demographics' and the rendered PDF puts Figure 3 four pages later. Why, and what is the fix? **Answer.** LaTeX defers floats when placing them at the source location would create awkward white space or break a paragraph, sometimes by pages. Two fixes, best combined. Use `fig-pos: "H"` (with `\usepackage{float}` in the header) to force exactly-here placement, for documents that must be read linearly. And refer to the figure by its cross-reference (`see @fig-demographics`) rather than by a typed 'Figure 3', so that the number and the link are correct wherever the figure lands. ::: ### Exercises 4. In a Quarto PDF with three tables, make every table appear exactly where it is declared. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Set the option once for the format and load the package: ```yaml format: pdf: tbl-pos: "H" header-includes: - \usepackage{float} ``` Verify in the PDF that each table follows the paragraph that precedes it in the source. A table that still floats was probably produced by a package that writes its own LaTeX float environment (for example `kableExtra`), which needs that package's option (`latex_options = "HOLD_position"`) instead. ::: ## Engines and other languages {#sec-rmd-workflow-engines} Quarto chooses an engine from a document's executable cells. A document with any `{r}` cell runs under knitr, which also runs Python cells through the `reticulate` package; a document whose executable cells are all Python runs under Jupyter; and an `engine:` key in the YAML overrides the choice. `knitr` documents support every chunk option you know from R Markdown, in either syntax. For most R work, the engine choice is invisible. With `reticulate` (R and Python) and `JuliaCall` (R and Julia), chunks can pass values across languages in one render: ````qmd --- format: html --- ```{{r}} library(reticulate) x <- 1:10 ``` ```{{python}} import numpy as np arr = np.array(r.x) print(arr.mean()) ``` ```{{r}} print(py$arr) ``` ```` In Python, `r.x` reads R's `x`; in R, `py$arr` reads Python's `arr`. Common types (numeric vectors, data frames, lists) convert automatically. Whether a mix is *helpful* depends on whether the languages do genuinely different jobs, such as R for the statistics and Python for a deep-learning model. For a typical biostatistical analysis, stay in one language: each additional one is another runtime to install, pin, and debug. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A `.qmd` with a `{python}` chunk renders correctly on your machine. A colleague clones the repository, runs `renv::restore()`, and the render fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`. What went wrong, and what would have prevented it? **Answer.** `renv` pins R packages. It says nothing about Python, so the document depended on whatever interpreter and packages happened to be installed on your machine, which is exactly the ambient state the book argues against everywhere else. It worked for you by accident of history: you had `pandas` from some earlier project. The fix is to declare the dependency in the document, so that provisioning is part of the build rather than a precondition of it: ```r reticulate::py_require("pandas") ``` Modern `reticulate` reads those declarations and provisions an ephemeral environment, which means the requirement travels with the source. The alternative many projects reach for, a `requirements.txt` plus an instruction to run `pip install -r`, is weaker for a reason worth generalizing. It puts the requirement in a file the render does not read, so nothing enforces the connection, and the failure appears on someone else's machine rather than yours. A dependency the build declares is checked on every render; a dependency documented in a README is checked when someone reads the README. ::: ### Exercises 5. Build a `.qmd` that computes one number in a Python chunk through `reticulate`, declares its Python packages with `py_require()`, and uses the number in the prose. Verify that the number is faithful to the same computation in R. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} Read the Python value back into R and compare it with the R computation in a chunk that stops the render if they disagree, for example `stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(py$arr_mean, mean(1:10))))`. Exact equality (`==`) is the wrong test for floating-point results computed by two runtimes; `all.equal()` allows for the last-digit differences they can produce. Render once in a fresh session to confirm that `py_require()`, not an interpreter already on your machine, supplied the packages. ::: ## Troubleshooting a render {#sec-rmd-workflow-troubleshoot} A render fails in one of two ways. The loud failure stops it with an error and a message that names the chunk; the silent failure finishes, exits successfully, and leaves a defect in the output. @tbl-rmd-render-failures collects the common ones; the worked example after it shows how to read a real log. | Symptom (message excerpt) | Cause | Fix | |---|---|---| | `Error: ! object 'x' not found`, then `Quitting from doc.qmd:14-18 [label]` | The object is created in a chunk that did not run (`eval: false`, or deleted) or runs later | Read the `Quitting from` line for the failing chunk; make the defining chunk run, and run before it | | `could not find function` | A package is used but not loaded in the document | Add the `library()` call to the document's setup chunk; the render runs in a fresh session | | `Unable to resolve crossref @fig-x` (a warning), and `?@fig-x` in the output | A missing or misspelled label, a label without its `fig-` or `tbl-` prefix, or a chunk that did not run | Fix the label; grep the output for `?@` (@sec-rmd-workflow-migrate) | | `\@ref(fig:x)` printed literally in the output | A `bookdown` reference left unconverted | Rewrite as `@fig-x` (@tbl-rmd-vs-quarto) | | `No TeX installation was detected` | PDF output needs LaTeX | `quarto install tinytex` | | `LaTeX Error: File ... .sty not found` | A LaTeX package missing from a minimal TeX installation | Install it (`tinytex::tlmgr_install("float")`, with the package's name), or let TinyTeX install it on the next render | | `ModuleNotFoundError` in a Python chunk | Python packages not declared | `reticulate::py_require()` (@sec-rmd-workflow-engines) | | `unknown writer` or an unknown format | A misspelled `format:` name, or a Quarto older than the format | Check the name; run `quarto check` and update Quarto | | Figures pages away from their citation | LaTeX float placement | `fig-pos` (@sec-rmd-workflow-floats) | | Every render slow | Expensive chunks re-run every time | `freeze` or `cache` (@sec-quarto-freeze) | | Old numbers after new data | `freeze` or `cache` served stored results | Render the document itself (@sec-quarto-freeze) | : Common rendering failures. The first two block the render; the next two finish with a defect in the output. {#tbl-rmd-render-failures} ### Worked example: a render that fails, then succeeds wrongly The example renders a one-figure HF-HOME report in a temporary directory, with two defects planted from real conversions: a setup chunk left at `eval: false` from drafting, and a figure label that kept its R Markdown name. It runs the real `quarto` command, so the log below is what you would see.[^r-libs] [^r-libs]: As in @sec-quarto-worked, the `env` argument passes this session's library paths to the R process that Quarto starts. In a terminal you would type `quarto render report.qmd` alone. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome") dbg <- file.path(tempdir(), "debug") unlink(dbg, recursive = TRUE) dir.create(dbg) trial <- merge( read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")), read.csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"), colClasses = c(patient_id = "character")), by = "patient_id" ) write.csv(trial[c("patient_id", "arm", "event_30d")], file.path(dbg, "trial.csv"), row.names = FALSE) doc <- c( "---", "title: 'HF-HOME: primary outcome'", "format: gfm", "---", "", "```{r}", "#| label: setup", "#| eval: false", "d <- read.csv('trial.csv')", "obs <- d[!is.na(d$event_30d), ]", "risk <- 100 * tapply(obs$event_30d, obs$arm, mean)", "```", "", "@fig-risk shows the observed risk in each arm.", "", "```{r}", "#| label: risk", "#| fig-cap: 'Observed 30-day risk by arm'", "barplot(risk, ylab = 'Risk (%)')", "```" ) render_doc <- function(doc) { writeLines(doc, file.path(dbg, "report.qmd")) r_libs <- paste0("R_LIBS=", paste(.libPaths(), collapse = .Platform$path.sep)) log <- suppressWarnings(system2( "quarto", c("render", file.path(dbg, "report.qmd")), stdout = TRUE, stderr = TRUE, env = r_libs )) status <- if (is.null(attr(log, "status"))) 0 else attr(log, "status") log <- gsub("\033\\[[0-9;]*m", "", log) log <- sub("^WARNING \\(.*\\) ", "WARNING ", log) list(status = status, log = grep("Error|^!|Quitting|WARN", log, value = TRUE)) } ``` ::: Render it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} first <- render_doc(doc) first #> $status #> [1] 1 #> #> $log #> [1] "Error:" #> [2] "! object 'risk' not found" #> [3] "Quitting from report.qmd:16-20 [risk]" #> [4] "WARN: Error encountered when rendering files" ``` ::: The render failed (a non-zero status), and the log says why in two lines. Read it from the bottom up. `Quitting from` names the file, the source lines, and the chunk label of the chunk that failed, here `risk`; the error above it names what that chunk could not find. The object is defined in `setup`, which never ran. The fix is to let it run: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} doc <- doc[doc != "#| eval: false"] second <- render_doc(doc) second #> $status #> [1] 0 #> #> $log #> [1] "WARNING Unable to resolve crossref @fig-risk" ``` ::: The status is now zero, and a build script or continuous integration would report success. The log still carries a warning: `risk` is not a figure label, because it lacks the `fig-` prefix, so the reference in the prose resolved to nothing. Look at the sentence Quarto wrote: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} grep("shows the observed", readLines(file.path(dbg, "report.md")), value = TRUE) #> [1] "**?@fig-risk** shows the observed risk in each arm." ``` ::: This is the silent failure, and it is the more expensive of the two: the first defect stopped the render, and this one shipped. Rename the label: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} doc <- sub("#| label: risk", "#| label: fig-risk", doc, fixed = TRUE) third <- render_doc(doc) third #> $status #> [1] 0 #> #> $log #> character(0) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} A render is done when the status is zero, the log has no warning, and the output contains no unresolved reference. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} out <- readLines(file.path(dbg, "report.md")) stopifnot( third$status == 0, length(grep("WARN", third$log)) == 0, !any(grepl("?@", out, fixed = TRUE)) ) grep("shows the observed", out, value = TRUE) #> [1] "Figure 1 shows the observed" ``` ::: The first two conditions are the log; the third is the output, and it is the one that would have caught the opening's PDF. ::: When a failure is not in @tbl-rmd-render-failures, reduce it. Copy the document, delete chunks and prose until the error disappears, and restore the last thing you deleted; what remains is a minimal example, usually under twenty lines, that either shows you the cause or is ready to post to the Quarto discussion forum. `quarto check` reports the versions of Quarto, R, knitr, and LaTeX that belong in any such post. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} A model is good at reading a render log, provided you give it the right excerpt and forbid the fixes that hide the error. > **Context.** A Quarto document fails to render. Below are the > last 30 lines of the log, the chunk named in the `Quitting > from` line with the chunks before it that define its inputs, > and the output of `quarto check`. > > **Constraints.** Do not suggest `error: true`, `eval: false`, > `warning: false`, `try()`, or reinstalling Quarto or R unless > the log shows a version problem. Change as few lines as > possible. > > **Criteria.** Name the line that fails and the cause, and say > what the log shows that supports the diagnosis. After your fix, > the render exits with status zero, the log has no `WARN` line, > and the output contains no `?@`. *Failure mode.* The suggested fix silences the symptom, by skipping the chunk or tolerating the error, and turns a loud failure into a silent one. *Check.* Apply the fix, re-render, and run this section's Verification on the output. A log and chunk code are structure; if the error message prints data values, cut them before sending (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** In the worked example, the second render exited with status zero. Why is a zero status not enough to call a render correct, and what two further checks does the Verification add? **Answer.** A zero status means the document compiled. Quarto treats an unresolved cross-reference as a warning, so a document can reach a reader with `?@fig-risk` in its prose and a successful build behind it. The Verification also requires a log with no warning and an output with no `?@`. ::: ### Exercises 6. A render log ends with these lines. Which chunk failed, what is the likely cause, and where do you look first? ``` 4/9 [fit-model] Error: ! object 'analysis_set' not found Quitting from paper.qmd:61-70 [fit-model] ``` ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} The chunk labeled `fit-model`, at lines 61 to 70 of `paper.qmd`, uses `analysis_set` before anything has created it. Look first at the chunk that should define `analysis_set`: it is set to `eval: false`, it comes after `fit-model`, or it was deleted. If the document reads `analysis_set` from a file or a pipeline target, check that the reading chunk ran. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 8: a clean render is not a correct render.** After every conversion or migration, grep the output for `?@` and compare figure and table numbers with the old build. 2. **Habit 3: version control from day one.** Migrate on a branch, and leave anything tagged at submission on the toolchain that produced it. 3. **Habit 4: pin the environment.** Declare every language's packages in the document (`py_require()`) or the lockfile, not in a README. ## Cumulative practice 7. *Cumulative (uses @sec-quarto).* Convert a short `.R` script of yours to `.qmd` with `knitr::spin()`, add one captioned figure with a cross-reference to it, and render to HTML and PDF. Apply the Verification of @sec-rmd-workflow-troubleshoot to both outputs. 8. *On your own work (no key).* Find an R Markdown analysis of yours that is finished and published. Write a short argument for *not* migrating it, in terms of what migration would and would not change about its reproducibility. ## Cheat sheet | Task | Code | |---|---| | `.R` to `.qmd` (`#'` prose, `#+` options) | `knitr::spin("a.R", knit = FALSE, format = "qmd")` | | `.Rmd` to `.R` | `knitr::purl("a.Rmd", documentation = 0)` | | `.Rmd` to `.qmd` | `git mv a.Rmd a.qmd`, then `knitr::convert_chunk_header("a.qmd", output = "a.qmd", type = "yaml")` | | `.ipynb` to and from `.qmd` | `quarto convert notebook.ipynb` | | Find unconverted references | `grep -rn '\\@ref(' --include='*.qmd' .` | | Find unresolved references | `grep -rn '?@' _book/` | | Force a figure in place (PDF) | `fig-pos: "H"` with `\usepackage{float}` | | Force a table in place (PDF) | `tbl-pos: "H"` | | Declare Python packages | `reticulate::py_require("pandas")` | | Report versions for a bug report | `quarto check` | : Migrating and troubleshooting at a glance. {#tbl-rmd-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@xie2020cookbook], *R Markdown Cookbook*, the recipe book. - [@xie2016bookdown], *bookdown: Authoring Books and Technical Documents with R Markdown*, for long-form documents. - Quarto's `quarto convert` documentation for `.ipynb` to `.qmd` conversion, and the knitr help page `?knitr::convert_chunk_header` for `.Rmd` chunk headers. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-12} 1. `knitr::spin('script.R')` is the canonical fast path: it turns a commented `.R` file into an `.Rmd` by treating any comment starting with `#'` as prose and everything else as code chunks. For `.qmd`, the same convention works with `knitr::spin('script.R', knit = FALSE, format = 'qmd')`. 2. LaTeX treats figures and tables as floats and rearranges them by default to avoid bad page breaks. `fig.pos = 'H'` (requires the `float` package) and `tbl-pos: 'H'` in Quarto YAML tell LaTeX 'place this exactly here, no reflow'. In chunks, `fig.pos = 'htbp'` means 'try here, then top, then bottom, then a float page' in order. 3. Use Quarto's cross-reference system: a `fig-` label on the figure (`#| label: fig-scatter`) plus `@fig-scatter` in the prose. Quarto handles HTML and PDF (and Word) anchoring with the same source syntax. Hand-rolled `\label{}` / `\ref{}` works only in PDF. The Quarto syntax is the durable choice.
